title: AO3’s takedown exposes divisions within its community | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

On October 29, the fan fiction site Archive of Our Own, more commonly known as AO3, unexpectedly went offline. Would-be visitors landed on a page saying it was shut down for maintenance, and a message on the AO3 Tumblr page said the work would take at least 12 hours — longer than routine upkeep but not necessarily cause for alarm. An update posted hours after that estimated that service restoration to the site would instead take two weeks, or potentially up to four.

Users were distraught at the prospect of a month without reading, or adding to, the site’s trove of stories imagining famous fictional characters in unlicensed and frequently uninhibited new plotlines and relationships. AO3 launched in 2009 and has since become one of the biggest fan fiction platforms on the internet. There are more than 18 million pieces of “fanworks” on AO3 and the site is home to large and dedicated fandom communities busily reworking figures from sources including Marvel, Harry Potter and the Japanese manga series “My Hero Academia.”

Now the archive has gone offline due to a site security breach that is still under investigation. Naomi Novik, one of AO3’s co-founders, said that she felt a sense of “resignation” when she learned of the hack.

“Right now, thanks to the irresponsibility of AI companies, virtually the entire tech world is being slammed at once and having to get fixes in at a breakneck speed,” she said, noting that dealing with security breaches is more difficult for a volunteer-run operation like AO3.

The platform doesn’t collect users’ personal information, so it seemed less likely to be targeted for a break-in. Novik said her team has confirmed stories posted to the site have not been deleted in the hack.

Devoted members of the AO3 community have been beside themselves since the site went down. “if ao3 is really going to be down for the next two weeks we gotta go back to oral storytelling around a crackling fire fertile crescent style or something man i can’t live like this,”one person wrote on X.

“how much longer is ao3 down im serious im having withdrawals,”posted another.

Desperate for their fan fiction fix, some took matters into their own hands and uploaded thousands of works into publicly accessible Google Drives. Many readers were grateful, but some writers were infuriated by what they saw as a violation of community norms.

The principles of how fandoms operate are delicate. While fan fiction on AO3 is free and openly accessible, writers still consider the works they post there personal and proprietary. Many even blanch at their stories being hyperlinked by outsiders since those fictions, from their perspective, belong in the community and not in the wider world.

“people couldn’t wait patiently till AO3 is back so they started treating fic writers like horrible villains, stealing their works, publishing without permission on tiktok and other platforms and feeding it to AI. this is just heartbreaking and horrible,” one writerposted on X.

“I think the speed and scale of the off-site sharing was startling and surprising to a lot of authors, who felt like their work was being wildly thrown around without their consent,” said one fan fiction writer who writes about video game characters and wished to remain anonymous.

Monia Ali, who writes the newsletterFandom Exilewhich analyzes the dynamics of fan communities, added that “a lot of people are on edge” because of their work being publicized and shared outside the intended website .

“Obviously, these works are all public,” Ali said. “But I think there are people who, once they’re done with a fandom, they want to delete all their works and they never want it to be accessed by anyone else. They don’t want there to be any remnants of it online.”

Prior to forums like AO3, many online fan fiction communities were scattered, explained Ali. She said that the diffused nature of those fan fiction communities often led to fanworks disappearing from the internet.

“People would let these individual sites lapse and those stories are gone forever,” she said. “What AO3 did was give people a place to import all of those works and restore it so there’s a complete history of a given community.”

Unlike other popular fan fiction sites like Wattpad, AO3 doesn’t sell ads or have a recommendation algorithm. It also doesn’t censor content, which has made it a popular forum for steamy stories that involve superheroes, fictional athletes and monsters. Some of those heated, homespun personal projects have grown into major commercial successes: Ali Hazelwood’s romantic novel “The Love Hypothesis” started as Star Wars fan fiction on AO3 and wasrecently adapted into a film. The 2025 hit novel “Alchemised” by SenYinLu is a rewrite of their wildly popular Harry Potter fanfiction “Manacled.”

Since authors are barred from selling works derived from other intellectual property — SenYinLu needed to change “Manacled” significantly in order to publish “Alchemised” and not run afoul of copyright law — many writers viewed writing fan fiction as a joyful hobby supported by dedicated fanbases. Now that literary agents and film producers are scouring platforms looking for their next hit, a rift has developed in the community, between commercially minded writers and the dedicated amateurs.

“People realized there’s a market for this stuff, and they can figure out where the fandom is or where the highest engagement is and then funnel that into development,” said Ali.

Not everyone is happy about how the wider fan fiction community has changed. “I’m realizing way too many people went into writing fanfiction thinking it worked like influencers and content creation. Fanfiction is for fun. Not attention, not engagement, not for profit. It’s for love a piece of media enough to write your own twist and if people like it cool,”wrote one fan fiction writer on X.

Others think that fan fiction is becoming just another consumer product, akin to the infinite stream of content on Netflix or TikTok. “People flip through without really thinking, it’s just a way to fill free time,” said one fan fiction author who specializes in anime and wished to remain anonymous because of fears of online backlash. “There’s a person behind these passion projects, but a lot of people don’t care. It’s a form of consumerism that come into fandom spaces.”

“I think a lot of authors have started to feel like they’re being treated like a content-churning machine instead of a fan sharing their thoughts with others,” the video game fan fiction author said.

AO3’s extended downtime has shown how sharp the conflict can get, and how the various fan fiction subcommunities rely on the site to hold things together. It also made it clear that for how insulated these fandoms might be, they are still subject to threats from the outside.

In the days after the site went down, several copycat platforms popped up with near-total scrapes of the forum, including, some users said, never-published drafts and deleted stories. On November 1, three days after the hack, a website called AO3.life appeared and included thousands of stories that had previously been on AO3. Many had been converted into purchasable AI-generated audiobooks.

Some of the largest clone sites have been shuttered after being bombarded with takedown notices from angry writers. There are even apology notes from the creators that have replaced the scraped archives. “It was never and is not my intention to hurt authors, and I hope every subsequent action I’ve taken is representative of that,” wrote the creator ofAO3.life, who identified himself as Ganesh, a 17-year-old based in India.

It’s not the first time fan fiction has been repackaged and sold. In 2024,404 Media reported thatsellers on Etsy were scraping works from sites like AO3 and turning them into physical books, with some costing as much as $100.

The combined forces of AI, the extractive nature of modern fan fiction, and frustrations over copyright and ownership have created a conflagration in the community. “Everything has just gotten bigger,” said the anime fan fiction writer. “There were a lot of people who cared about but didn’t speak up about these issues, and then when AO3 went down everyone just started panicking.”

Novik said the site will be back up soon. “I’m not worried about AO3 itself because our tech team are amazing heroes who keep one of the top 20 sites in the world running on 30 Altairian dollars a day in their free time,” she said. “I just hope they don’t run themselves ragged to get it up quicker.”
